title: Sharp logarithmic growth of the Bapat–Sunder eigenvalue ratio
shortTitle: How far the Bapat–Sunder eigenvalue can exceed the permanent
oneLine: The largest eigenvalue of the Bapat–Sunder matrix F_A can exceed the permanent by a factor of about (1/2) log n for real and log n for complex n × n matrices, already at real rank three and complex rank two, with an exactly checked 27 × 27 integer example.
abstract: For a positive semidefinite matrix A of order n, the matrix F_A with entries a_ij per A(i,j) has every row sum equal to the permanent per A, so per A is one of its eigenvalues; in 1986 Bapat and Sunder conjectured that it is the largest. Counterexamples are known over the complex numbers (Drury) and the reals (Chalmers, rank four, order 32), but how large the ratio B(A) = λ_max(F_A)/per A can be was open. This candidate shows that its largest value over correlation matrices of order n is (1/2) log n over the reals and log n over the complex numbers, each up to an error of order log log n, with explicit upper bounds (1/2) log n + 5/2 and log n + 5. Real matrices of rank three and complex matrices of rank two attain these values; with the real rank-two theorem of a recent preprint, reproved in full in an appendix, three is the smallest real rank at which the inequality fails, answering a question of Chalmers. Exact-arithmetic certificates give a real counterexample of rank three and order 27 with integer vectors and B > 1.0036, and finite examples with B > 1.32 (real) and B > 2.64 (complex) at order 378 and B > 2.17 and B > 4.34 at order 10710. For every higher permanental compound C_k with k ≥ 2, the inequality for 0/1 test vectors stated by Pate (2008, Theorem 7) fails without bound; it is true for k = 1 (Pate's Corollary 3), and an explicit 0/1 vector for k = 2 gives the ratio 1.1508. Lev's inequality already gives the order O(log n) once the 0/1 bound is known; new are the sharp constants, the matching construction, the minimal ranks, the order-27 witness and the higher-compound result. The upper bound combines a layer-cake inequality with Lieb's theorem on block permanents; the lower bound realises polynomials whose roots lie on concentric circles as products of linear forms in low-rank Gram matrices. Limits: first-order constants only; the minimal real order is open (at most 27); the optical reading assumes an idealised Gaussian-delay model. AI-assisted, unrefereed candidate; no external peer review, independent reproduction or formal verification is claimed.

keyResults: Theorem 1.1 (proof, main): for large n, (1/2) log n − C₀ log log n ≤ b_R(n) ≤ (1/2) log n + 5/2 and log n − C₀ log log n ≤ b_C(n) ≤ log n + 5, where b_K(n) is the largest ratio λ_max(F_A)/per A over n × n correlation matrices over K; the lower bounds are attained at real rank three and complex rank two.

Corollary 1.2 (proof, main): the smallest rank with λ_max(F_A) > per A is three over the reals and two over the complex numbers; the real rank-two exclusion (liqsweep) is reproved in full in Appendix A. This answers Chalmers's minimal-rank question.

Proposition 2.4 and Lemma 2.1 (proof): B(A) ≤ 4d_n (complex) and 2d_n (real), with d_n < 5/4 + (1/4) log n, from Lieb's theorem on 0/1 vectors and a layer-cake inequality whose constants are asymptotically optimal (Remark 6.1).

Corollary 7.1 (proof, main): for each k ≥ 2, the 0/1 inequality for the permanental compound C_k stated in Pate's Theorem 7 fails, with R(C_k(D)) ≥ c_k (log n)^{k−1} per D; it holds for k = 1 (Pate's Corollary 3).

Section 8 (exact certificates): a real rank-three witness of order 27 with integer Gram vectors and B > 1.0036; real rank-three B > 1.32 and 2.17 and complex rank-two B > 2.64 and 4.34 at orders 378 and 10710; a 0/1 test for C_2 at order 21420 with ratio > 1.1508.

narration:
This is an audio briefing from Evidence Press on a research candidate about how far a matrix eigenvalue can rise above a quantity called the permanent.

The permanent is the determinant's sign-free cousin: add up the products of a matrix's entries along every permutation, with no minus signs. Take a table of inner products of vectors, a positive semidefinite matrix. From the permanents of its smaller pieces one builds a companion matrix whose rows all add up to the permanent, so the permanent is one of its eigenvalues. Bapat and Sunder asked whether it is always the largest eigenvalue.

The question also has a physical meaning. For photons passing through an interferometer, the chance that they all bunch into a few output channels is a permanent, and an eigenvalue above the permanent means that small time delays between the photons can raise that chance.

Counterexamples were already known, but nobody knew how large the violation could get. For matrices of size n, the worst ratio of the top eigenvalue to the permanent grows like one half of the natural logarithm of n for real matrices, and like the full logarithm for complex matrices, with explicit bounds that match up to a smaller correction. Real matrices of rank three and complex matrices of rank two already reach these values, so three is the smallest real rank at which the conjecture fails. The paper also gives a checkable integer example of size twenty-seven, smaller than the previous record, and shows that a related inequality of Pate fails without bound for higher compounds.

For the upper bound, the proof tests the matrix on simple zero-one vectors and rebuilds every other vector from layers of those. For the lower bound, it places the roots of a polynomial on circles of growing size, and each circle adds the same amount to the eigenvalue.

The limits are clear: only the leading constants are sharp, the smallest real size of a counterexample is open, and the optics concerns an idealised model, not an experiment.

This is an unrefereed candidate, checked by internal AI-assisted review and exact computer arithmetic rather than by peer review, and this briefing uses a synthetic voice that is not additional evidence.

relatedWorks.citation: Bapat and Sunder (1986), An extremal property of the permanent and the determinant. Linear Algebra and its Applications. The conjecture that per A is the largest eigenvalue of F_A (their Conjecture 3), its place in the Schur power problem, and the case n ≤ 3.
Djoković (1969), Simple proof of a theorem on permanents. Glasgow Mathematical Journal. Lieb's theorem on block permanents, used here exactly as stated and proved there.
Drury (2018), A counterexample to a question of Bapat & Sunder. Mathematical Inequalities & Applications. The first counterexample, complex, of order eight and rank two.

Lev (2015), Discrete norms of a matrix and the converse to the expander mixing lemma. Linear Algebra and its Applications. A general inequality that, with the 0/1 bound, already gives B(A) = O(log n).
Pate (2008), On permanental compounds. Linear Algebra and its Applications. The 0/1 inequality for k = 1 (Corollary 3), true, and for every k (Theorem 7), shown here to fail for every k ≥ 2.
Seron, Novo and Cerf (2023), Boson bunching is not maximized by indistinguishable particles. Nature Photonics. Bunching probabilities as permanents, the setting of the optical interpretation.
